articles.title: Judge tosses Trump’s lawsuit against Wall Street Journal again, this time for good
articles.summary: A federal judge on Saturday dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on a lewd birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein bearing Trump’s name.
articles.body: A federal judge on Saturday dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on a lewd birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein bearing Trump’s name. US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles ruled that Trump failed to plausibly allege that the Rupert Murdoch-owned newspaper acted with “actual malice” when it published the story. Gayles rejected the president’s argument that The Journal should have withheld its story after he denied writing the letter, saying such a requirement would violate the First Amendment. “Were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press,” the judge wrote. The ruling is another stinging defeat in the president’s legal crusade against the American news media and is sure to be celebrated by the press freedom groups that have denounced Trump’s suits. Gayles previously dismissed the $20 billion lawsuit in April, ruling that Trump’s original complaint relied on “formulaic” assertions of malice that came “nowhere close” to the legal standard for a public figure. But the judge dismissed the case without prejudice and gave Trump an opportunity to file an amended complaint addressing those shortcomings. In Saturday’s ruling, Gayles found that Trump’s revised complaint still failed to resolve those issues and dismissed the case with prejudice. “We’re pleased with the court’s decision,” a spokesperson for Dow Jones, the Journal’s parent, told CNN. When asked for comment, the White House referred CNN to Trump’s personal lawyers. CNN has reached out to the president’s legal team. Trump sued The Journal, its parent companies, Murdoch and two reporters in July 2025 after the newspaper reported on the sexually suggestive letter. Trump denied writing it and accused The Journal of knowingly publishing a false story. The case was especially unusual because Trump brought it while serving as president. Legal analysts who spoke with CNN said they could not recall another instance of a sitting president suing a news outlet over a story. However, it was also part of a recognizable, long-running pattern for Trump — using the courts to pressure news organizations over unflattering coverage of him. During his second term, Trump has also filed a $15 billion defamation case against The New York Times over its coverage of his 2024 campaign. A judge dismissed the original complaint last year but allowed Trump to refile. In July, the judge deferred a decision on the Times’ motion to dismiss and directed Trump to revise his complaint again, which he did in August. Late last year, Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over its editing of his January 6, 2021, speech in a documentary about the Capitol attack. The British broadcaster has vowed to defend the case in court. One month before taking office, Trump sued Iowa pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling company, The Des Moines Register and its parent company, over a poll released days before the 2024 election showing him trailing Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in Iowa. A judge dismissed that lawsuit with prejudice in September. Legal experts have deemed these lawsuits frivolous and full of holes, but warn that winning may be besides the point for Trump: The publicity and threat of protracted litigation can pressure news outlets and chill aggressive reporting. articles.title: FBI says North Korea was behind the $6.3 billion Binance crypto hack
articles.summary: Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea.
articles.body: Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea. Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. Crypto prices fell Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe. The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Teng said Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT Saturday, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.
